questions.prompt: What are the four things a published finding from this repo must contain?
options: A post, a chart, a tag and a link
The raw runs, the report, the announcement and the licence
The repo, the command to run it, the raw evidence, and the one finding
The hypothesis, the plan, the run and the conclusion
questions.explain: That package is what lets a stranger check you: the repo says what was measured, the command says how to reproduce it and what it costs, the raw runs/*.jsonl is the evidence, and the one finding is the sentence under test. The tempting wrong options each contain pieces of the real thing - a report is derived rather than raw, a hypothesis and a plan are the private road to the result rather than the result, and a link without the other three is a request to trust you.

questions.prompt: What does the rule "runs/*.jsonl - committed raw evidence, append-only" forbid?
options: Adding a new run to the directory
Editing or deleting a committed raw run file - including deleting a run whose result turned out to be wrong
Committing two runs of the same battery
questions.explain: Append-only means the record only grows: you add runs, you never edit them and you never delete them. The tempting case is the one the rule exists for - if a result later proves wrong, the correction is appended (a new entry in the decision log, a note in the write-up) while the original run stays, because deleting it would leave the repository looking better than it is. The other options are all ordinary practice: new runs, derived reports and repeated batteries are exactly what the folder is for.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in the five-minute review you run before publishing?
options: Recompute one number by hand from the raw .jsonl and check that the run id in the write-up resolves to a file in runs/
Rewrite the finding so that it reads more confidently
Delete the runs that are not interesting before publishing
Remove the SIMULATED RUN banner from a mock report so it reads cleanly
questions.explain: The review is a set of checks a reader could carry out too: identifiers resolve, numbers recompute, the mock is labelled, the n is stated, no credential is committed, the repo's own gates pass, and the decision log has the entry. The tempting wrong answers are the three classic ways a publication goes wrong - editing for confidence, curating away inconvenient evidence, and removing the warning that stops a harness test being read as a model evaluation. All three destroy the thing that made the number checkable.

questions.prompt: Your experiment found no effect at all. What do you publish?
options: Nothing - a null result is not a result
Only the hypothesis, so that nobody repeats the experiment
The same package - repo, command, raw evidence - with a finding sentence that reports no effect
A short summary of the null run, without the raw files
questions.explain: A null result is checkable in exactly the same way as a positive one, and it is often the more valuable publication - it stops the next person spending a week and a few dollars re-running it. The evidence contract does not change: same repo, same command, same raw files, one sentence that reports what was and was not found. The tempting first option is the habit this lesson is trying to break - treating a flat result as a failure rather than as a result; the second and fourth options drop exactly the parts that make it checkable.
